newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Goldman sees U.S. stocks rally continuing in 97/98.
newsitem.headline: Goldman sees U.S. stocks rally continuing in 97/98.

text.p: The bull market that has swept U.S. share prices to record levels is expected to continue throughout 1997 and 1998, Steven Einhorn, partner and head of global investment research at Goldman Sachs, said on Wednesday.
But he said while U.S. equities could produce average annual returns of about 10 percent over 1997 and 1998, Europe, Latin America and Hong Kong should produce better returns.
"It is our clear sense that we have another two years at a minimum left in this particular (U.S.) bull market expansion," he told a presentation on the U.S. equity market outlook.
"Over the next 12 months, or for the full year 1997, we expect U.S. shares will deliver a total return of roughly 10 percent," said Einhorn.
"Our preliminary expectations will be that in 1998 shares can again deliver a low-double-digit total rate of return."
However, Einhorn said Goldman was underweighted in the United States in its global portfolio "believing that Europe and Latin America in particular will deliver better returns".
Goldman's single most favorite market in Europe is Germany.

"We are overweighted in Europe expecting that over the course of the next 12 months, if the U.S. does 10 percent, Europe can do 13 to 15 percent, principally on the back of more significant earnings growth," he said.
He said Europe "should deliver double the earnings growth that we will deliver in 1997."

In emerging markets, Goldman has been overweighted in Latin America, Mexico and Brazil but is more cautious on Asian emerging markets, excluding Hong Kong, due to a slowdown in economic activity. Hong Kong stocks were likely to do better than U.S. shares due to more substantial profit growth and flows of money from the United States, said Einhorn.

Globally, Goldman has an above-average weighting in equities and a below-average weighting in bonds. In its U.S. portfolio, Goldman has an allocation of 65 percent equities, 20-25 percent bonds and 10 percent cash and commodities.
Einhorn said the Dow industrials could reach 6,200 before the end of the year and 6,700 to 6,800 during 1997.
He said 10 percent growth in U.S. share prices in 1997 would be comprised of about eight percent earnings growth for S&P 500 companies and a dividend yield of about two percent.

He expected the U.S. economy to grow throughout the remainder of 1996, all of 1997 and all of 1998. "We believe the growth will be moderate, roughly two and a half percent, neither too strong generating problematic inflation nor too weak to bring about earnings disappointments in any systematic way."
Einhorn said U.S. inflation has been well contained and expected a rise to about three percent from 2.7 percent in 1996.
